## Findings by module

### 1

- **confirmed** (Casement report, chunks 1 to 5: depopulation observed): Casement's report of 11/12/1903 (Africa No. 1, 1904) is a British consul's firsthand account of a 2.5-month journey on the Upper Congo in 1903, comparing places he knew in 1887: Lukolela about 5,000 then, under 600 now (a careful enumeration); Bolobo about 40,000 in early days, now 7,000 to 8,000 (believed); the F* villages 4,000 to 5,000 then, now no more than 500; Montaka 4,000 ten years ago, now 600 to 800; the lake-side towns of Mantumba down 60 to 70 per cent in ten years. These are observed local reductions, not a country-wide count, and he assigns causes jointly: sleeping sickness and smallpox, flight to French territory, hunger, and the methods used to extract rubber and food. This gives the Module 1 toll lesson a primary source for the 'about half' premise at local scale, and for the disease argument. He himself says sleeping sickness takes 'a prominent place' but that natives attribute decline principally to other causes.
- **confirmed** (Casement report: mutilation seen first-hand): Casement says he personally saw two mutilated people at Lake Mantumba: a young man whose hands had been beaten off against a tree, and a boy of 11 or 12 whose right hand was cut off at the wrist; of six mutilated during the rubber regime, five had died by the time of his visit. He also quotes an officer's diary entry (an invalid on his way home, who died soon after) saying that a cartridge expended had to be accounted for by a right hand, and that 6,000 cartridges were used in six months on the Momboyo; Casement 'cannot vouch' for the entry but heard it from an officer of standing. This matches Hochschild's Simon Roi item (finding of 6,000 cartridges) and gives the course a primary basis for 'hand-cutting was a system of proof', with the caution Casement himself uses: first-hand for two cases, second-hand for the rest.
- **refined** (ch-005.txt (Lansdowne memorandum of 06/06/1904, footnotes)): British rebuttal: the 500 and 240 figures name two different groups of villages; the prosecutor was the Company's guest and Epondo retracted at the Company's headquarters on 08/10/1903 after swearing the opposite the day before; a witness said to have fled actually testified on 08/10; the stump was not fully healed on 07/09/1903, against 'a long time ago'; Epondo takes under a page of Casement's 39 and about half of the State's reply. Calls for an independent commission.
- **extended** (Casement report: how extraction worked, with his own arithmetic): He documents the 'prestations' (weekly and fortnightly food and labour taxes) set by decree (6/10/1891, 5/12/1892, 28/11/1893), the illegal fines imposed on villages, imprisonment of defaulters without trial, the Force Publique estimated at not less than 18,000 men, concession companies with 'droits de police' (Circular of 20/10/1900) and armed forest guards, the A.B.I.R. concession with a yield of 600 to 800 tons in a good year and 58 Europeans, and examples such as one village's weekly levy (value 132 francs, paid 21.30 francs) which he totals over the year: 6,864 francs given and 1,107.60 received (our arithmetic: 132 x 52 = 6,864 and 21.30 x 52 = 1,107.60, both correct). He also reports children sold to pay a fine of 55,000 rods (2,750 francs). Use one case as a worked example of checking an official's figures.
- **extended** (Casement report: his stance and limits): Casement opens by crediting real achievements (steamers, a railway, ending open slave markets) and is cautious about native statements he finds 'of such a nature that I could not believe them to be true' until the people's flight and the facts corroborate; names are masked with letters (A*, B, C) in this printed version, which is the stripping of names that Hochschild says the Foreign Office imposed. Placed beside the course's 'Casement's 1904 report' sentence: the report is dated 11/12/1903, was printed as Africa No. 1 in early 1904, and is a consul's evidence in a diplomatic format, not a court record. It also describes the people as 'savages' and 'cannibals' in the colonial language of its day, which should be flagged to learners.
- **extended** (Casement report: concession system, hostage women and the Wahis circular): At Bongandanga (A.B.I.R. concession) he saw a fortnightly 'market' where 242 men from one village each owed 3 kg of dried rubber (about three quarters of a ton in all; our arithmetic: 242 x 3 = 726 kg), watched by armed sentries, with a 'maison des otages' for defaulters and women seized to force husbands to bring rubber or meat. He puts what a man received for a fortnight's rubber at goods worth under a shilling against rubber worth about 2 pounds (his valuation: 7 kg at 7 francs a kilo), twenty-six times a year. He cites the Governor-General's circular of 29/03/1901 pressing officials to raise rubber yields and says a rifle count shows 550 rifles and many cap-guns for one concession and not less than 10,000 armed men across the concessions, plus a Force Publique of not less than 18,000. This corroborates Hochschild's mechanism (quotas, hostages, concession police) from a primary source and gives the question 'who was responsible' an answer: officials and companies, with the Government 'cognizant and responsible'.
- **extended** (Casement report: African testimony and its limits): Casement records statements from villagers and mutilated children, some taken through interpreters: a 15-year-old boy whose left hand was cut off, which he proved on the spot by confronting the sentry (the one case he could verify and later reported to Coquilhatville), two boys of 6 to 7 with right hands gone, men shot while refusing a rubber levy, and a headman fined 10,000 rods and forcibly moved by the Commissaire-General. He says everything asserted by such people 'strictly true' he would not claim, but that their previous silence said more than their speech. So the report is also a source of African voices, as recorded by a European and an interpreter, which refines Hochschild's remark that few African voices survive in writing. Casement's language ('savages', 'cannibals') is of its time and should be flagged.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt (Inclosures 1 to 4)): Casement first doubted the refugees' account ('a tale which I cannot think can be true', and 'doubtless exaggerated') and then found corroboration in missionary letters and State sentries. Statements were taken through interpreters and signed before him; mission witnesses countersigned.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt (Inclosure 2, Whitehead letters)): Rev. John Whitehead, Lukolela: 'not less than 6,000' in January 1891 (an estimate), 719 counted at the end of December 1896, 352 counted in July 1903; he puts quite half of riverine deaths down to sleeping sickness and links fear, hunger and compulsory food and rubber supply to the rising death rate. Also a weekly tax of 900 brass rods' worth of manioc bread from 160 women.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt (Inclosure 3)): Missionary table for 14 villages on Lake Mantumba: 12,320 people in 1893 and 1,610 in 1903 (careful estimates), a fall of 87 per cent; four named causes of the fall (war and killings, weakened bodies and hunger, mortality of children sent to missions, fewer births) and an estimate that 99 per cent of the wars arose from failure to supply produce, labour or men.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt (Inclosures 5, 7, 8)): Governor-General Wahis circular 20/10/1900 says company 'right of police' was misread and used for the gravest abuses; 07/09/1903 circular admits armed soldiers were being sent out under black NCOs against standing orders; 29/03/1901 circular presses for more rubber and 'unceasing efforts to increase production' as prices fell.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt (Notes of 12/03/1904, Annexes 1 to 3)): Congo State reply: attacks Casement's population figures, blames sleeping sickness, smallpox, migration and the end of the slave trade (Mgr Van Ronsle), says he travelled with Protestant missionaries and was seen as a redresser of wrongs, relies on a prosecutor's inquiry into the Epondo case (boar bite; witnesses fled; Epondo retracted 08/10/1903) and compares the labour tax with Rhodesia (19,653 of 56,700 huts paying in labour, 4,938 in produce).
- **extended** (ch-005.txt (Nightingale despatch 07/04/1904, judgment of 15/03/1904)): Boma Court of Appeal: Caudron guilty of premeditated murder as moral author (Liboke night of 15 to 16/10/1902; expeditions January to March 1903 ordered to fire on villagers to raise rubber), unpaid tax and obedience to superiors no defence, no law then authorised the company to demand rubber as tax; sentence cut from 20 to 5 years with extenuating circumstances; Jones 10 years upheld with a hope of early release; local government refused to produce political reports. Nightingale's covering note wrongly says 15 years; the judgment says five. Verified deaths '122' is his hearsay.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt (trade table)): Bulletin Officiel table: exports 15,146,976 francs in 1897 and 50,069,514 in 1902 (3.3 times), imports 21,181,462 and 18,080,909; the British memorandum argues rising exports with falling imports and a falling population mean the producers were not paid; the Governor-General's own circulars show the guns came through State channels.
- **note** (ch-005.txt (judgment, Congo State reply)): Both the reply and the judgment use racial language about Africans as a reason to doubt testimony or to mitigate sentences; teach it as part of the source, not as evidence.
